issues.description: The problem statement instructs students to initialize the SealSaloon attributes (orders and stock) in the constructor, but elsewhere requires that the stock attribute be static and final (shared across all instances). Initializing a static final shared stock in an instance constructor conflicts with the static/final requirement and is implementation-wise misleading. This contradiction can confuse students about where/how to initialize the shared stock (in the constructor per earlier instruction, or as a static final field/static initializer per the static requirement).
issues.suggestedFix: Clarify the problem statement so it does not ask students to initialize the static final stock in the constructor. Either (A) require that only the orders array is initialized in the (instance) constructor and specify that the shared static final stock should be initialized at declaration or in a static initializer, or (B) change the requirement so stock is not static/final and thus can be initialized per-instance in the constructor. This removes the contradictory instructions while preserving the intended design.

issues.description: The getter for the StockIngredient name is named differently between the template and the solution. The template defines getIngredientName() (src/de/tum/cit/ase/StockIngredient.java) while the solution uses getName() (src/de/tum/cit/ase/StockIngredient.java). The problem statement asks students to "add getters for all the private fields" but does not prescribe the exact getter name, which leaves an inconsistent mapping between starter code and reference solution and may confuse students about which getter name to implement and use across Stock and other classes.
issues.suggestedFix: Use a single consistent getter name for the StockIngredient name across artifacts. Prefer renaming the template's getIngredientName() to getName() and update all references in Stock and other classes (e.g., Stock.findStockIngredient) to call getName(). Alternatively, change the solution to use getIngredientName(), but ensure the problem statement notes the expected getter name to avoid ambiguity.
